metadata.title: Fan Out: Coordinating Dozens of Agents in Parallel Without Blocking
metadata.subtitle: One Call, Many Sessions
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register (Feynman × MKBHD): how does a single agent coordinate dozens of parallel sub-agents without opening multiple conversations or blocking the flow? Lands the carry-out that fanning out is one call that spawns isolated sessions the server waits on and merges — not multiple chats stitched together by hand — and judges the design choice that pushes the wait into the server instead of the caller.

beats.narration_text: Liam, in for Bear. Look at that question on screen — it's the wrong frame. Fifty separate conversations means fifty chat windows you would juggle by hand. That is not what happens. One call, and the server spawns the sessions itself. So how does that actually work?

beats.narration_text: The problem is coordination without blocking. One agent, many sub-agents running long work in parallel, no side conversations to babysit. How does the head stay coherent while the workers work?

The obvious guess: open three chat windows, run a query in each, paste the results into a fourth chat to merge them. Fine for a demo. At fifty analysts, that model collapses under its own copy-paste — you become the bottleneck.

shot.new_visual_element: THREE SEPARATE CHATS, COPIED BY HAND

production_viz.caption: you open them, you copy the results yourself

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A custom tool — dispatch analysts — is registered as the orchestration trigger. The head agent calls it with a list of tickers. The server intercepts that call. It does not run the analysis itself; it spawns three independent analyst sessions, each with its own full context window, each running in parallel. The head pauses. The server watches the workers. When all three return, it wakes the head with the accumulated results. Fan out, fan in. The server is the coordinator; the agent is the caller.

Watch the concrete flow. The head of research receives the prompt: sweep NVDA, AMD, and MU, rank by margin durability. It calls dispatch analysts with the three tickers. The server intercepts. Three analyst sessions spawn simultaneously. Each independently reads twenty pages of SEC filings, scores on a rubric, returns a grade. The head is not blocking your terminal, not locking the conversation — the server is watching all three in the background. When they finish: NVDA scores nine, AMD scores six, MU scores four. The head wakes, reads the accumulated table, synthesizes a ranked report. One conversation. Three parallel analysts. One merged report. That is the whole design choice — the wait moves into the server, not into you.

Isolation is the mechanism. One call becomes N parallel sessions. Each session is fully sealed — its own context, its own tools, its own errors. Nothing leaks across. They rejoin when they finish, not when the head decides to poll. The server coordinates; the agent just calls.

The timing gap here is categorical, not incremental. Serial execution: fifty analysts, thirty seconds each, one after another — twenty-five minutes. Parallel fan-out: fifty analysts dispatched simultaneously, and the whole batch finishes in the time the slowest one takes. About thirty seconds. Serial is a queue. Parallel is a wave. What you pay for is the coordination overhead. What you buy is a fifty-times collapse in wall-clock time.

The results don't merge themselves. Each session returns a chip: ticker, score, findings. The chips arrive at different times. The aggregator is a dumb collector — it holds the chips until the last one lands, then runs three operations: deduplicate, rank by score, merge into one structured report. Not smart. It just refuses to hand back a partial answer.

Both sides obey a fixed contract. The head sends a task ID, ticker, and query focus. Each analyst returns a task ID, findings, confidence, and sources. The aggregator checks every result against that shape. An off-schema result is rejected on its own — one broken session cannot corrupt the rest. Skip the contract, and one bad session silently poisons the merged report. The schema is what makes the isolation hold.

props.sparkLine: Fixed schema in. Fixed schema out.

beats.narration_text: Fanning out is not more chats. It is one call that spawns isolated sessions, the server waits on them, and the aggregator merges the results.

props.quote: Fanning out isn't opening more chats. It's one call that spawns isolated sessions the server waits on, and merges for you.

beats.narration_text: Here is a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Ask it to design a parallel fan-out orchestration for auditing ten stocks — the tool signature the head calls, the fixed contract each worker returns, and what the aggregator does when one worker returns off-schema data. Go deeper: what breaks first when one worker takes ten times longer than the median — the aggregator, the head's context window, or your patience?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand parallel fan-out orchestration for LLM agents. A head agent calls one custom tool that spawns N isolated worker sessions in parallel; each worker has its own context window, runs independently, and returns a structured result; an aggregator merges the results and wakes the head. Design this orchestration for auditing a portfolio of ten stocks in parallel. Specify: (1) the tool signature the head calls, (2) the fixed schema each worker returns (fields and types), (3) how the aggregator handles workers that finish at different times, (4) what happens when one worker returns off-schema data, and (5) what happens when one worker takes ten times longer than the median. Give this as pseudocode plus a short design note naming the trade-offs you made.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what breaks first under a heavy-tailed latency distribution — the aggregator's memory as it holds partial results, the head agent's context window when the merged report finally lands, or the user's patience — and how would you redesign the aggregator to fail gracefully on that tail (partial merge? timeout budget? speculative retry?) without sacrificing the schema guarantee that keeps the isolation intact?
